Construct M, P, D on the respective lines OA, OB, OC, on the opposite side of O and at equal distance (a point equal to O remains O). Thus M=2O-A, P=2O-B, D=2O-C. If O lies on the supporting line AB, the image segment has that same supporting line but equals the original segment only when O is its midpoint (with the obvious collapsed-segment exception). When O is off it, the image boundary is a parallel line at twice O's original boundary distance and the inequality reverses. source_reviews.independent_solution: A centrally symmetric figure is a point set F for which some O satisfies Z_O(F)=F. This is setwise invariance, not pointwise fixing. Examples include a segment about its midpoint, a circle about its center, a parallelogram about its diagonal intersection, a line about every point on that line, and the union of two intersecting lines about their intersection.

source_reviews.independent_solution: A nondegenerate segment has its midpoint as unique center; a line has every point on it as a center; a ray has no center; a circle has its center; the union of two distinct intersecting lines has their intersection as unique center. For genuine nondegenerate simple polygons, a half-turn pairs vertices without fixed vertices, so the number of vertices is even: no triangle or pentagon exists, while a quadrilateral does exist (a parallelogram). This is an existence statement, not a claim that every quadrilateral is symmetric. A line or the whole plane has more than two centers, indeed infinitely many. Conversely, a nonempty bounded figure cannot have two distinct centers: composing their half-turns produces a nonzero translation, whose iterates would make the figure unbounded.

source_reviews.independent_solution: A compass-only construction works for every B, including both the segment and its exterior. If B=O, return O without drawing a zero-radius circle. Otherwise put r=OB, draw Gamma=C(O,r), and draw C(B,r), obtaining two intersections; select either as C. Draw C(C,r); its intersections with Gamma are B and D, so select D other than B. Draw C(D,r); its intersections with Gamma are C and B', so select B' other than C. Each chord has length r and subtends 60 degrees on Gamma; always taking the other intersection walks three steps consistently around the circle, making B' the point opposite B and O the midpoint of BB'. All steps use only a compass and already known intersections. Endpoint cases B=A or A_1 return A_1 or A, respectively, and collinear exterior points also work. For an independent distance check, B' must satisfy AB'=A_1B and A_1B'=AB; for collinear B these circles are tangent (apart from zero-radius endpoint cases), while off the line one must disambiguate the two intersections rather than choose arbitrarily.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Let O be the vertex of two vertical angles, each formed by two opposite pairs of rays. The half-turn about O maps the two sides of one angle to the two sides of the other, preserves their angles, and therefore maps its unique internal bisector ray to the other angle's internal bisector ray. A half-turn sends a ray based at its center to the opposite ray. The two bisectors are consequently opposite rays lying on one line through O, not identical directed rays. The original asks for a proof, whose generation is an additional capacity beyond recognizing this argument.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For equal-radius circles with centers O_1 and O_2, a half-turn about their midpoint M sends O_1 to O_2 and, as an isometry, sends the entire first circle onto the second. For the two complementary half-planes bounded by one line, a half-turn about any point on that boundary preserves the boundary and swaps its two sides, hence maps one entire half-plane onto the other and proves congruence. If two designated half-planes are actually the same, identity suffices. Open/closed boundary membership is preserved. The proof concerns a whole point-set image, not only equal-looking outlines.
